curation.lead:
Records show that on January 25, 2019, Reid Weingarten asked Jeffrey Epstein for “special jeffrey insights” about Rajeev Misra while considering representation [HOUSE_OVERSIGHT_028576][Finding #13272]. Records show that the following day Weingarten discussed possibly using Ron Soffer for what he called the “Softbank caper” [HOUSE_OVERSIGHT_028576][Finding #13272]. Review of the records identifies prospective-client and lawyer-vetting discussions; the records do not state that Weingarten or Soffer was retained [Finding #13272].

In separate correspondence on January 26, Epstein asked Brad Karp of Paul Weiss whether he represented Misra, and Karp first replied, “Sort of” [EFTA02627034][Finding #13074]. He then wrote, “Spoke to him yesterday” [EFTA02627034][Finding #13074]. Twelve minutes later Epstein told Weingarten, “brad represent softbank, not rajeev, but did speak to him yesterday, re DB” [HOUSE_OVERSIGHT_028577][Finding #13163]. Cross-reference of the two messages shows that the categorical SoftBank/not-Misra wording and unresolved “DB” reference were Epstein’s words, not Karp’s; the records do not independently establish the conversation’s subject or a personal Misra engagement [Finding #13163].

An archived November 6, 2018 Paul Weiss biography listed SoftBank among Karp’s recent clients in significant securities, commercial, and regulatory matters [Finding #13162]. The listing does not identify the matter, scope, billing client, or Misra as a personal client [Finding #13162]. In a separate 2025 FTX multidistrict-litigation matter, Karp appeared for four Temasek-related defendants; SoftBank entities were other parties in the broader litigation but were not named as his clients in that appearance [Finding #13249].

sections.title: January 2019 Legal-Contact Exchanges
sections.content:
Analysis of records shows that on January 25, 2019, Reid Weingarten asked Epstein, “Rajeev misra....softbank vision fund...any special jeffrey insights here?” and Epstein answered, “If he wants you to rep him. YES” [HOUSE_OVERSIGHT_028576]. Cross-reference of the record shows that, in the following day's discussion about French-Israeli lawyer Ron Soffer, Weingarten wrote that Misra “wants me to hire him” and that he was “thinking about using him on the Softbank caper”; Epstein replied “go slow,” and the later request to “get the book on him” concerned Soffer, not Misra [HOUSE_OVERSIGHT_028576][Finding #13272].

At 1:00 p.m. EST on January 26, Epstein separately asked Brad Karp, chair of Paul Weiss, “Rajeev misra do you represent?” and Karp first replied, “Sort of” [EFTA02627034][Finding #13074][Finding #13163]. He then wrote, “Spoke to him yesterday” [EFTA02627034][Finding #13074][Finding #13163]. At 1:12 p.m., Epstein relayed to Weingarten, “brad represent softbank, not rajeev, but did speak to him yesterday, re DB” [HOUSE_OVERSIGHT_028577][Finding #13163]. The stronger SoftBank/not-Misra formulation and “re DB” therefore came from Epstein; the documents do not identify what “DB” meant or independently prove the subject or status of Karp's conversation with Misra [Finding #13163].

After Epstein's relay, Weingarten wrote, “obviously don't mention my role with brad till we both think it useful” [HOUSE_OVERSIGHT_028577][Finding #13074]. Review of the records does not establish that Weingarten or Soffer was retained and does not show that Karp knew of their discussion or joined a common mandate [Finding #13272][Finding #13074].

sections.title: Representation and Attribution Limits
sections.content:
An archived November 6, 2018 Paul Weiss biography listed SoftBank among Karp's recent clients in significant securities, commercial, and regulatory matters [Finding #13162]. The listing does not identify the matter, engagement dates, billing client, or Misra as a personal client [Finding #13162].

Karp's January 2019 “Sort of” reply documents a recent conversation with Misra but does not identify a mandate, advice, or formal engagement [EFTA02627034][Finding #13074]. A four-record comparison documents different Paul Weiss contexts and personnel; it does not itself establish a shared team, cross-matter information flow, or privilege breach [Finding #13233].

A separate 2025 FTX multidistrict-litigation entry personally names Karp for four Temasek-related defendants; SoftBank entities appear elsewhere in that litigation, but the Karp appearance does not name them as his clients [Finding #13249].

curation.system_role: The retained record places Misra within a narrow set of prospective-client, lawyer-vetting, and representation-status exchanges. It separates Karp’s exact reply from Epstein’s stronger relay and distinguishes documented firm-level SoftBank work from unproven personal representation of Misra.
open_questions: What engagement, conflicts, billing, or calendar records identify the subject and status of Karp's January 25, 2019 conversation with Misra [Finding #13074]?

What did Epstein mean by ‘DB’ in his January 26 relay, and what source beyond Epstein's message supports or contradicts the SoftBank/not-Misra characterization [HOUSE_OVERSIGHT_028577][Finding #13163]?
Did Weingarten or Ron Soffer open a matter, perform work, or bill Misra after the January 25–26 discussion [HOUSE_OVERSIGHT_028576][Finding #13272]?
What matter, dates, scope, and billing client underlay the archived Paul Weiss listing of SoftBank among Karp's recent clients [Finding #13162]?
Which lawyers represented the SoftBank entities named elsewhere in the FTX MDL, and were their matters related to the Temasek defendants represented by Karp [Finding #13249]?

citation_findings.summary: Document metadata places Epstein’s receipt of Karp’s ambiguous Misra reply at 1:00 p.m. EST on January 26, 2019; Epstein relayed a stronger characterization to Reid Weingarten at 1:12 p.m., twelve minutes later.
citation_findings.detail: Karp answered “Sort of. Spoke to him yesterday” when asked whether he represented Rajeev Misra. Twelve minutes after the source document’s date-received timestamp (1548525600 = 18:00 UTC = 1:00 p.m. EST), Epstein told Weingarten “brad represent softbank, not rajeev, but did speak to him yesterday, re DB.” The categorical SoftBank/not-Misra formulation and “re DB” appear in Epstein’s relay, not in Karp’s written reply; they therefore cannot be treated as Karp’s exact words or as independent proof of the engagement or call subject. “DB” remains unresolved.

citation_findings.summary: Four source records document distinct Paul Weiss contexts involving Leon Black, a Gates Foundation consultation, Melinda French Gates divorce counsel, and firm scale; those records alone do not establish a common team or cross-matter information flow.
citation_findings.detail: The attached records show: Leon Black engaged Southern Trust Company to assist his advisers at Paul Weiss and McDermott; Morgan Lewis scheduled a Gates Foundation-related call with Paul Weiss contacts; the 2021 Gates divorce petition names Bruce Birenboim and Loretta Ippolito for Melinda French Gates; and a Paul Weiss release described a firm of more than 1,000 lawyers. These records show different contexts and personnel. They do not by themselves prove or disprove a broader cross-matter team, information flow, privilege breach, or the separate Ghosn, SoftBank, and Caesars matters.

citation_findings.summary: A January 2025 CourtListener docket entry personally names Karp for four Temasek-related defendants in the FTX multidistrict litigation; SoftBank entities appear elsewhere in the MDL party list, but the Karp entry does not name them as his clients.
citation_findings.detail: Docket entry 809 adds Karp for Artz Fund Investments Private Limited, Blakiston Investments Pte. Ltd., Temasek International (USA) LLC, and Temasek International Private Limited. The broader MDL metadata includes SoftBank II Tempest (DE) LLC, SoftBank Investment Advisers (UK) Limited, SoftBank Group Corp., and SoftBank Global Advisers Limited as other parties. The record therefore supports a personal Karp-to-Temasek legal edge, not a Karp-to-SoftBank edge.
